author: Robert Narai
title: Days of hope and rage in France
content:
At the centre of Paris, the Monument à la République looms over a square that has hosted every great mobilisation of the French left in modern history. The bronze statue of Marianne, symbol of the Republic, holds an olive branch above the words: 

Liberté. Égalité. Fraternité.

 During mass demonstrations on 17 October, dozens of young people scaled the monument while tens of thousands looked on. Some flew Palestinian and red flags. On the statue of 

Egalité

, someone had scrawled “jeunesse dorée” (“gilded youth”, an old term for the idle rich). Marianne herself was draped in a giant yellow vest bearing the words: “The police mutilate high school students”.

For almost a month now, a mass student revolt has been rocking France, in one of the deepest political crises seen in the country in decades. The state that claims to embody liberty, equality and fraternity has answered 

lycéens

 (high schoolers aged 15 to 18) demanding better conditions in schools with tear gas, rubber bullets and mass arrests. That the Republic’s police are maiming young people in the streets is an indictment of the capitalist system the Republic protects.

Days of rage

In response to a national day of action on 17 October, in which an estimated 800,000 people protested across France, the government of Emmanuel Macron unleashed a flurry of violence.

Police fired tear gas into the crowd gathering at Place de la République before the march had formed. Riot police armed with batons, shields and armoured vehicles charged into crowds in Paris, Lyons, Bordeaux and a string of provincial cities, attacking protesters and bystanders alike. According to the Interior Ministry, almost 1,800 people were arrested and more than 500 police were injured, with 855 arrests in Paris alone. A teenager lost a hand in Saint-Étienne and another lost an eye in Mulhouse. Street medics were dragged along the ground by police.

The new element on 17 October was the return of the Yellow Vests, the leaderless movement of rural and provincial workers against fuel taxes and the high cost of living that erupted in 2018, until it was crushed with brute force by the state. After weeks of watching 

lycéens

 face down riot police, the Yellow Vests called their own day of action protesting the cost of living. The Yellow Vests blocked roundabouts and fuel depots from the morning and declared their support for the student revolt. Among them was Pierre, a retiree from Bandol: “I’ve been gassed five times since this morning”, he told 

La Provence

. “[Macron’s government] is declaring war on the people.” The return of the Yellow Vests raises the possibility of the student revolt becoming a rallying point for broader working-class grievances.

Nurses, teachers and firefighters joined the Yellow Vests demonstration. In Lille, 20 rail workers marched together in their SNCF vests. Most of the working class support the movement (55 percent of the French population support the student-led protest movement, according to an Elabe poll) but are not yet part of it.

Whose Republic?

The Macron government’s strategy has been to paint the victims of violence as its perpetrators. Prime Minister Lecornu blamed “far-left groups”, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez targeted “ultra-left individuals”, while Macron declared that “nothing can explain, nothing can excuse” the violence. They pointed to a handful of burnt buildings, such as the town hall in Limoges, to paint a movement of hundreds of thousands as a mindless mob. “The perpetrators directly targeted the institutions of the Republic and the authority of the State”, wrote Bordeaux mayor Thomas Cazenave.

It is worth asking what sort of Republic the mayor of Bordeaux is defending: one in which a burnt town hall causes enormous outrage, but a sixteen-year-old losing an eye to a police grenade prompts hysteria about the need for more law and order.

The ruling class never calls the conditions that produced this revolt violence. Students in France’s poorest schools sit in classrooms infested with cockroaches and rats, in classes of up to 35. Outside school, the police stop, search and arrest young Black and Arab men from the 

banlieues

 (working-class suburbs) for the colour of their skin and the estate they live on, and their operations now cause more than one death per week. Fuel and food prices keep rising, while, according to Oxfam, 53 billionaires own as much as the poorest 48 percent of the population. This is the systematic violence the working class is subjected to every day under French capitalism.

“A riot is the language of the unheard”, as Martin Luther King Jr said. The looting that broke out in some cities is not senseless. It comes from people with little money who have been demonised for years and told that their lives are worthless.

Yet riots are not a way forward for the movement. They invite more repression and hand the right the story it wants to tell, of mindless “casseurs” (wreckers) to be answered with curfews and soldiers. And they push away workers whose strikes could win what the movement wants.

The right has also racialised the riots. Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon blamed 

racaille

 (“scum”) and “

that 

type of population”, while fascist Éric Zemmour, leader of the far right Reconquête, described “a horde of Maghrebi and African barbarians entering the cities”.

The impact of this racist backlash can be seen in the 

banlieue

 of Trappes. On 23 October, a gunman drove through the Parisian suburb for around fifteen minutes, shooting at black and brown people. He killed a 26-year-old and wounded several others, among them a 12-year-old girl who was shot eight times. 

Le Monde 

reports that he “congratulated himself, in essence, on having ‘avenged the shopkeepers’” by attacking “Blacks and Arabs”. Politicians across the spectrum, Macron included, have professed their horror, but these are crocodile tears from the people responsible for the climate of racism. For years, they have backed laws against migrants, refugees and Muslims and echoed the politics of the fascist National Rally. 

Polarisation

This is not the first time that working-class youth from the 

banlieues

 have rebelled against the French state. In 2005 and again in 2023, after police killings of teenagers, the suburbs rose without the workers’ movement: much of the left abandoned the rioters in 2005, and in 2023 the union leaders offered only statements, not strikes.

What has changed in 2026 is that the youth have learned lessons from previous struggles. This revolt began in the schools, not as a riot, and its first act was to create mass assemblies through which students can democratically direct their movement. And it has been shaped by two experiences less evident before. The first is the Palestine movement, which taught a generation about state repression and the moral vacuum at the heart of the Republic. The second is the fascist National Rally, who, if they come to power in next year’s presidential elections, pose a mortal threat to the interests of all workers and the oppressed.

The threat of a fascist-led Republic gives the student revolt a sense of urgency and a sharper political edge: students are not only demanding a better future, but defending the right to have one at all. And years of mass strikes have taught them where the power to win lies: with the workers who can shut down production.

The revolt is also radicalising the capitalist class. “A wave of shock has swept through the business world”, writes Martine Orange in 

Mediapart

. “We have a useless, unworthy, incompetent political class”, an investment banker told Orange. “Retailleau, Attal, Philippe, Glucksmann [leading politicians of the centre and right]—there isn’t one of them worth anything.”

Many capitalists are looking for an iron fist that can restore profitability and order. France’s public debt is well above 100 percent of GDP, and the ruling class want workers to pay the bill: first, the budget cuts the students are blocking, then further attacks on pay, pensions and public services. That will require defeating the unions and the left. While many capitalists do not entirely trust Marine Le Pen (presidential candidate and leader of the RN), Orange concludes, “some believe she alone will be able to ‘restore the authority’ they crave”.

The fascist Le Pen is ready to do the job. Her party has spent years courting big business and presenting itself as the party of order. An RN government would not have to build the repressive machinery for a confrontation with the unions and the left, because the centre has already built it: bans on demonstrations, the power to dissolve left-wing organisations, and riot police and soldiers normalised and ready to be deployed against the population. Macron is currently wielding it against high schoolers and youth from the 

banlieues

. A Le Pen presidency could wield it against unions and the left.

For decades, the French establishment has told voters that the “Republican Front” of the centre is all that stands between the Republic and the fascist RN. They say that the only way to keep out the fascists is to vote for the establishment candidate and accept their austerity and racism. Macron and his allies have used this argument repeatedly to bludgeon the left into voting for them. In 2024, the New Popular Front, an alliance of the left including France Unbowed that challenged this logic, won the most seats only for Macron to refuse to let the left form a government. The defenders of so-called “Republican values” are throwing open the doors of the Élysée to the fascists.

In the days after 17 October, the Macron government set about building a de facto state of emergency without openly declaring one. Lecornu gave mayors the power to impose curfews “where they need to”. Curfews on minors followed in Paris and other major cities. Protests were banned, and the army’s Sentinelle patrols were deployed. “If necessary, clearly we could”, said Lecornu when asked about declaring a state of emergency. At the same time, he invited the RN to meetings on the government’s crisis response. By the eve of 24 October, the ban had spread to nearly every city, and the government had mobilised 70,000 police, special forces and armoured vehicles.

Days of hope 

Since 17 October, the student assemblies have spread from the high schools to the universities. In Bordeaux, about 1,000 students packed each of two campus assemblies. In the Paris region, delegates from 32 campuses voted to join the days of action on 22 and 29 October and the march on 24 October, and to prepare for a general strike from 5 November.

On 22 October, the national coordination of student assemblies called a day of action in Paris, but the police turned the march into a static rally. 

The state could stop them marching on 22 October. But it could not stop them on 24 October. In a massive show of strength, hundreds of thousands of demonstrators defied the Macron government’s intimidation tactics. Hundreds of thousands of students and workers stretched over four kilometres in Paris. Tens of thousands marched in Marseilles where they held a minute of silence, hands raised, for the victims of Trappes and against fascism. In Bordeaux, more than 10,000 braved driving rain and defied a ban on demonstrating in the city centre. The cops responded with tear gas. In Lyons, around 20,000 marched in the face of armoured vehicles, as the police fired volleys of tear gas. In Nice, the police used water cannons to try to smash the demonstration. An estimated 800,000 people mobilised across the entire country. One placard in Paris summed up the contempt for the ruling-class hysteria over broken glass: “I would have liked to be a shop window, so I would be taken more seriously”.

24 October was a humiliation for the Macron government and a significant victory for the movement: the show of force was meant to intimidate people. Instead, it has only emboldened them. Macron’s government no longer knows whether it can contain the fury from below.

The day also saw tens of thousands take on the fascists in Orléans, where the RN held its congress to launch Le Pen’s presidential campaign under heavy police protection. More than 30,000 people marched, about twice as many as expected: trade unionists, young anti-racists, undocumented migrants, women’s and LGBT+ groups, and the revolutionary left. This is not enough on its own to stop the fascists winning state power, but it sent a clear message: the RN may be winning at the polls, but it cannot hold the streets.

In a major step forward for the movement, the country’s second-largest trade union federation, the CGT, has been pressured to call a general strike for 5 November. The intersyndicale, the coalition of France’s main union confederations, spent the weeks before 24 October asking the government for concessions on the budget and school funding, even excluding high school representatives from the negotiations. But Lecornu offered nothing, and now, deprived of their mediating role, they are calling for a general strike. “Workers must hold general assemblies everywhere, in all workplaces, with all their colleagues, in every administration, to generalize the November 5 strike and after”, CGT general secretary Sophie Binet said in a statement.

Macron’s dilemma is that if he continues to use repression to keep the students off the streets, he risks a social explosion. But if he relaxes his grip, the crisis of the budget and the school system returns, and the revolt continues to grow. 

The movement has its own dilemma. The state has shown it will make an example of anyone who steps out of line, and the threat of prison and curfews is enough to keep many demonstrators at home. At the same time, the union leadership holds the keys to the workers’ strength and uses them cautiously. Union leaders speak boldly while preparing for a bureaucratic one-day strike. A one-day strike would let off steam; it would not break the government. (In 2023, the union leaders called fourteen separate one-day strikes over five months, and Macron waited them out.) The answer is for workers to shut down production and halt the flow of profits by going on indefinite strike in their millions.

The Yellow Vests have called “Acte III” for 31 October, and high school and university students will keep pushing for national days of action on 29 October and use the school holidays to take the argument to hospitals, railway stations and workplaces to build their own assemblies. Anti-racist organisations and trade unions defied bans on demonstrations on 26 October in response to the racist attack in Trappes.

Students and workers have shown that the Republic’s iron fist can be defied through mass action. As 5 November approaches, the ability of the organised left to carry the students’ militancy into the workplaces, and to win workers to the rank-and-file action that can take a strike beyond a single day, will decide how far this rebellion goes.

author: April Holcombe
title: China’s forgotten miracle makers
content:
History has no parallel for modern China’s economic transformation. To what do we owe the China “miracle”, in which annual GDP growth averaged 9 percent over 40 years, wages up roughly tenfold in 30 years, and more high-speed rail built in ten years than the rest of the world in all time?

In the heyday of globalisation, people said China proved the magic of free markets and free trade. These days, people are more likely to attribute the country’s success to some special Chinese characteristic, such as its state-directed investment or its “Communist” dictatorship. 

These perspectives share in common a wilful or ignorant blindness to capitalism’s real wealth creators. Economic value comes neither from the market’s “invisible hand” nor the state’s “guiding hand”, but plain old everyday hands. The secret to China’s “miracle” is the not-so-miraculous condition of its working class.

Beginning in the 1990s, the greatest ever number of wage labourers was assembled through the collusion of profit-hungry foreign capital with millions of venal bureaucrats and their repressive state machine. Three hundred million people decamped from rural poverty to seek better lives in China’s cities, while urban compatriots in state-owned mines and mills lost their livelihoods through merciless privatisation.

China’s working class is legally stratified into “migrant” and “resident”, subject to the severest dictatorship of their bosses, and deprived of political rights to speak out or unionise. Apply hundreds of billions in Western and Taiwanese investments, lather, rinse, repeat for decades, and voilà! You have the most “miraculous” economic growth in capitalist history. 

China’s migrant workforce

We are used to hearing about how important migrants are to Western economies, but migration—the internal kind from village to city, not country-to-country—has been even more critical to China’s boom. In the 1990s, the government enticed young villagers with the prospect of independence, new experiences and better pay in newly established, deregulated Special Economic Zones with low wages and low taxes.

Lu Qingmin first left her family’s half-acre farm and came to Dongguan, a burgeoning megacity in the southern manufacturing heartland of the Pearl River Delta, in the early 2000s. Bosses preferred migrant women like her, considering them doubly docile. Writer Leslie Chang, in her 2008 book 

Factory Girls

, described Lu’s experiences at her first job in a Hong Kong-owned alarm clock factory:

“A day on the assembly line stretched from eight in the morning until midnight—thirteen hours on the job plus two breaks for meals—and workers labored every day for weeks on end. From the moment she entered the factory she wanted to leave.”

The Pearl River Delta opened wide to investment in such sweatshops, and American-style hyper-individualism flowed in with it. Self-help books, life-coaching gurus, pyramid schemes, talent markets, unregulated colleges: each refracted through the false prism of empowerment what migrant workers already felt in their bones: 

you are on your own

.

Hukou

: China’s internal visa system

Every migrant who left for the cities took the same thing with them: their rural 

hukou 

(户口), a residential registration that acts like an internal passport. Originally designed under Mao Zedong in 1958 to prohibit rural-to-urban movement altogether, the 

hukou 

household registration system was repurposed to create a pliant, defenceless workforce with second-class citizenship wherever it went.

Out-of-town 

hukou 

holders, also called the “floating population”, now represent just under half of the country’s workforce. Registered to villages far away, they are denied health insurance and pensions by the local government where they actually live. Many cities bar them from buying property, and local schools charge significant sums to teach their children. 

Think of them like the United States’ undocumented immigrants, who can get driver’s licences but not Social Security, who work in practically every key industry, but technically are not supposed to be there at all. Except there are now as many in China as the entire US population.

China does not offer the equivalent of America’s birthright citizenship: children inherit their parents’ 

hukou

 wherever they are born. Locked out by the prohibitive cost of urban schooling, tens of millions of “left behind” children grow up in the countryside with their grandparents, only seeing their parents once a year. 

The first generation of migrant workers (1992–2002) viewed themselves as temporarily itinerant farmers; the second (2003–15) identified as wage labourers from elsewhere. The third generation (2016–today) feel like urban natives except for the jarring fact of their 

hukou

. “Increasingly, if you walk around any cities in China, you won’t be able to tell who’s a migrant worker or not”, labour researcher Kevin Lin said. “There’s a pipeline from the technical vocational school into factories, but many others are college educated.”

Yet talk of 

hukou 

reform is just that; local governments simply save too much money by denying pensions, health care and education. As labour academic Eli Friedman explained in response to recent flowery statements by the State Council:

“Such a project [

hukou

 abolition] would need to be funded by taxes on the rich and capital. It could also drive up the cost of business and undermine China’s dominant export machine. It is precisely because deep 

hukou

 abolition entails profound fiscal and social reform that it has been quietly opposed, undermined, and diluted across the decades.”

Housing: the China dream?

Despite the headline figure of “90 percent home ownership” in China, between half and two-thirds of the migrant population are renting in cities far from the family home they “own”, according to a series of studies over the last decade.

“Urban villages” offer cheap, informally subdivided dwellings in once-rural outskirts now enveloped within city limits. Occupying a legal grey zone, residents in these neighbourhoods can face sudden eviction and demolition. Private developers build expensive new suburbs on the rubble, forcing migrants further out in cycles of gentrification familiar to residents of Sydney or New York City.

The Beijing city government went further in cleansing the whole capital of its “rat tribe”: people forced to rent out cellars, underground bunkers or even spaces inside walls. After a deadly fire killed nineteen people in 2017, officials launched an eviction drive of such ferocity that even Beijing’s urban residents, often seen as coldly indifferent to migrants’ plight, raised a public outcry. Many of the 120,000 evicted migrants had to sleep rough through the northern winter. The Communist Party made no dwellings available in the lavish gated communities or in the empty second properties owned by the city’s wealthiest residents. 

The factory dormitory system also lets companies extend labour hours and better monitor absenteeism, but workers cannot live with family, easily form relationships, or enjoy any privacy. Cramped quarters, however, can create stronger social bonds and explosive pressure, as in April 2014, when one retiring woman’s despair at finding that the Yue Yuen shoe factory had never paid into her social insurance triggered a ten-day strike of the entire complex’s 40,000 workers.

Rising wages and falling poverty

The most widespread defence of the Communist Party dictatorship is that, on its watch, 800 million people have been lifted out of absolute poverty. Undoubtedly, wages and living standards have risen sharply over the past 30 years. This is an inevitable, contradictory component of capitalist industrialisation, already analysed in Karl Marx’s 1861 work 

Capital

. Socialism requires workers’ democratic control over such explosions of new wealth to meet collectively determined needs. Instead, China has followed the same development path charted by anti-communist dictatorships in Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan.

For perspective, absolute poverty is a very low bar, since even rock-bottom wages are a lot of money for the poorest farming families. When one woman, Leiya, moved to Shenzhen in the early 2000s, she instantly became the family breadwinner. “She put together gift boxes for the factory’s clothing line, earning RMB 600 (US$70) a month, working from 8am to 2am”, Yuan Yang recounted in her 2024 book 

Private Revolutions

. “As a fifteen-year-old in the city, Leiya was already earning three times what the average farmer earned back home.”

Sending wages back to the village as remittances did most of the heavy lifting in raising living standards; it has similarly reduced absolute poverty in Pakistan, the Pacific Islands and the Philippines, as workers leave to be exploited in Australia or the Gulf monarchies. 

Industrialisation turned rural privation into something far more profitable and productive: urban wage labour. Figures for business profits, labour productivity and capital investment in China run rings around wage growth. This process of value extraction, which Marxists call exploitation, has benefited foreign investors, “Communist” bureaucrats and local billionaires and multi-millionaires. It has also buoyed a well-to-do middle class that is much more likely than the working masses to support China’s stabilising, profiteering dictatorship. 

Capitalist growth widened the wealth gap immeasurably faster than it reduced poverty. A 2022 report jointly produced by China’s Ministry of Finance and the World Bank found that the country’s Gini coefficient, a measure of income inequality, skyrocketed from 0.30 in the mid-1980s to 0.49 in 2008—that’s worse than the United States. China’s “semi-elasticity of poverty”, which measures the percentage reduction in the absolute poverty rate per percentage of GDP growth, was just 0.27. That means that, pound for pound, China reduced poverty 

less 

efficiently than Pakistan, South Africa or Indonesia.

Of course, there have been many, many more pounds. “More than the ability to translate growth into poverty reduction, it was China’s sustained fast growth that was unusual by international standards”, the report found. Eighty percent of all absolute poverty had been eliminated by 2008, over which time universal health care and social security had been utterly eviscerated.

Workers in state-owned enterprises

Over the same period, living standards for workers in state-owned enterprises (SOEs) also fell. Approximately 70 percent of SOEs were partially or completely privatised from 1990–2002, resulting in 60 million job losses. The resulting insecurity was a “big layoff stick waved over the head of any rebel workers”, wrote Fan Wendong, a militant distillery worker, in 

My Twenty Years in a State Enterprise

. Local bureaucrats, who once kept their jobs by hitting (or pretending to hit) production quotas, were now encouraged to get rich from the dirty work of mass sackings. The aim was not purely “efficiency”, but also to push managerial power even further out of workers’ reach. Fan wrote:

“Most of us were convinced that it was entirely possible that the factory could be run well if it wasn’t for the bureaucratic institutions ruining the operations. We workers never had the right to run our factories. All leadership positions in the enterprise were assigned top down, with the enterprise director post often filled by an inexperienced hand or even a crook.”

Company directors and party cadres forced workers to “buy into” the company before throwing them on the scrapheap, as Trotskyist Au Loong Yu described in a 2011 introduction to Fan’s book:

“Starting as a compulsory exercise to coerce workers into taking part in raising an enterprise’s capital, it would not be long before the enterprise would enter bankruptcy, perhaps by design, thus looting workers of their hard-earned savings in the process.”

Working hours: capitalism’s classic contradiction

The boom years, already pregnant with contradiction, gave way to slowdown. Over the past decade of declining wage growth, workers have raised their living standards only through inhuman, illegal and irrational amounts of overtime.

Inhuman because the average working week, at 48.2 hours or 9.64 hours per working day, is now the highest on record. The May 2026 figure from the National Bureau of Statistics is worse than the peak sweatshop era in 2005, and smashes contemporary averages for Japan, South Korea, and Vietnam of 36.6 hours, 37.9 hours and 41.5 hours, respectively. 

Illegal because the 2008 Labour Contract Law caps the working week at 44 hours. Yet bosses know that most workers cannot live without overtime. Suddenly implementing the 40-hour week is a new form of “disguised layoffs”, a claim made by 3,000 mostly women strikers at Shenzhen Yilisheng electronics factory in December 2025. What kind of system forces workers to strike for illegal overtime?

Irrational because hours in China are “polarising” between the overworked and underemployed, as the ILO details in its 2025 report 

Short Hours of Work, Long Hours of Work and Work Hours Mismatch in China’s Labour Market.

 Since a record 10 percent now work fewer than 20 hours weekly, the 42 percent who work “over 48 hours” includes tens of millions clocking 60, 70 and beyond. So 30 years of unparalleled economic development have not reduced the working day. Working-class life is still caught in the clutches of monstrous contradictions, condemned so long ago by Karl Marx in 

Capital

:

“Machinery in itself shortens the hours of labour, but when employed by capital it lengthens them. In itself, [machinery] lightens labour, but when employed by capital it heightens its intensity.”

Factory dictatorship

This heightened intensity shows up in brutal working conditions. Inside China’s gleaming new high-tech infrastructure—its modern offices, warehouses and factories—bosses have not stopped treating workers like absolute shit. 

Managers subject employees to verbal and even physical abuse, while docking pay for workplace infractions. A firm’s list of fineable offences can stretch to more than 100 behaviours and typically includes talking on the assembly line, using one’s phone, taking too long in the bathroom, production mistakes and taking too many sick days. 

Almost all factory workers suffer from work-related musculoskeletal disorders, but statistics cannot capture what migrant worker-poet Zheng Xiaoqiong could in her 2012 recollection of a 17-year-old workmate:

Fatiguehas become her only word of expression On the assembly lineher body is stiff and clumsy her joints acheher fingers are heavy like machines In her backlegs waist she has lost control of the indescribable painpressing her body like a rock 

With high turnover from stress and strain, bosses withhold workers’ first payment for two months as standard practice. Quitting before then means surrendering all wages, which some people still choose to do.

Labour law and trade unions: arms of the capitalist state

Most of the above violates the country’s 2008 Labor Contract Law. But the court system, expanded after a chilling crackdown on labour activism in 2015, is rigged against the workers. Bosses enjoy the upper hand in court as they do in life, winning 67 percent of unfair dismissal cases, according to a 2021 analysis of more than 2,000 rulings (employees win just 15 percent). Labour courts provide even less protection for those working without a contract, estimated at 85 percent of the 300 million in “flexible employment”. 

China’s official trade union movement is even more useless. The All-China Federation of Trade Unions is a government-controlled institution represented in workplaces by upper management. It has not endorsed a single strike since at least 1982, when the constitution removed the right to strike. During the 2010 Nanhai Honda dispute, a landmark struggle inaugurating China’s last strike wave, union officials led a hundred goons in physical clashes with picketing workers.

China’s unruliest subjects

The victimised, exploited Chinese working class is potentially the most powerful agent of change in world history. A lot of the Communist Party’s authoritarian rule is preoccupied with keeping this potential suppressed.

Hardline repression of strikes is neither practical nor wise. The state cannot expend resources and political legitimacy every year repressing thousands of labour protests. The party-state’s responsive flexibility, offering concessions in one hand and flashing the police baton in the other, is a source of great strength.

However, strike leaders are unfailingly, ruthlessly, single-mindedly identified, sacked and even arrested to prevent ongoing organising. Labour NGOs, which once helped educate and organise migrant workers, were smashed in 2015, with activists jailed and centres permanently closed. For China’s capitalist rulers, who still view comparatively low wages as their international competitive edge, the right to form independent trade unions is the reddest of red lines.

Partly a strategic adaptation to repression, partly a real feature of its atomisation, working-class struggles remain profoundly defensive and depoliticised. Strikes rarely raise overtly political slogans and mostly demand what they already have a legal right to. Of 240 recorded factory strikes in 2023, the 

China Labour Bulletin

 (which, under expanding state repression in Hong Kong, was forced to shut permanently in 2025) reported that 68 percent concerned unpaid wages. “Give us our blood and sweat wages!” is the most commonly heard chant.

This does not mean that strikes are tame. With safety in numbers, plenty of workers are willing to curse bosses, push on police lines, block highways and chant outside government or company buildings. 

In late November 2022, a riot shook Foxconn’s largest iPhone assembly complex in the city of Zhengzhou. The company’s COVID-zero “closed loop” system confined 200,000 people to work, eat and sleep in the factory. Pay frustrations and COVID fears resulted in a mass breakout attempt, with water cannon-wielding police fighting to hold back barricade-hurling crowds. Eventually, Foxconn, having lost US$7.4

 

billion in projected earnings, paid large bonuses to get the strikers to 

leave

. The pro-democracy White Paper protests began on a Shanghai street the very next day.

It is impossible to predict exactly when new waves of struggle will erupt from China’s working class. Yet the awesome power slumbering in its lap, the simmering frustration which here and there boils over in indignation, self-sacrificing courage and resourceful self-organisation, makes it all the more galling that some so-called leftists choose to support the country’s ruling party of exploiters instead.

China is home to 700 million workers. Those who hate capitalism must be able to look them in the face and call them—without caveat, hesitation or hypocrisy—our siblings in chains, our comrades in struggle, our world’s grandest hope for a new beginning.

author: Tom Sullivan
title: Review: Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser
content:
Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History

 by US writer and Pulitzer Prize winner Benjamin Moser is a useful contribution to uncover the history of opposition to Zionism within modern Judaism. It traces the history of anti-Zionism from the late 19th Century through the lives of several anti-Zionist Jews across the Middle East, Latin America, Africa, Europe and the US.

Moser begins in the late 19th Century in the Russian Empire, where the deep oppression that the Jewish population faced led to a cultural Zionism that, among other things, sought to revive Hebrew. One of its leaders was Aaron Samuel Tamares. But around the same time, there was also a territorial, national, and racial Zionism being developed by figures like Theodor Herzl. Published in 1896, Herzl’s 

Der Judenstaat

 (The State of the Jews) gave a racial definition to Jewish people, as opposed to the then-dominant idea of Jews being a religious community. It also argued that European anti-semitism could never be eradicated and an independent Jewish state was therefore necessary.

In response to Herzl, the cultural Zionism of Tamares and many other rabbis quickly became an explicit anti-Zionism. They were among the first to criticise how Herzl’s Zionism reinforced the existing anti-semitism of the time by defining the Jewish population as a “race” and “foreign elements” in their own countries.

Tamares did not reject Jewish communities in Palestine despite being an anti-Zionist. But he ferociously opposed the establishment of a Jewish state. To him, such a project was inextricably linked to Western imperialism. He asked why the European powers “should make recompense for 

their 

wrongdoings by handing over foreign property, 

Ottoman

land”?’

When the British began that process with the establishment of the British Mandate after World War One, the Zionist movement remained on the fringes within the Jewish population as it had when Herzl published 

Der Judenstaat

. In 1917, for example, Zionist groups in England had no more than four thousand members between them.

Moser describes the early days of the British Mandate through Jacob Israel de Haan. When de Haan emigrated from the Netherlands to Palestine in 1919, he was among the most prominent Dutch Zionists. But after seeing the violence of the Zionist groups against the indigenous population of both the Palestinian Muslims and Orthodox Jews, he quickly became a leading figure of the Agudah, an anti-Zionist, Orthodox Jewish organisation.

De Haan’s articles were some of the first to document the growing Zionist domination of Palestine in the early 1920s. He explained “that no Arab is allowed to live in Tel Aviv. That no Arab is received in a Jewish hotel. That companies in their statutes decide that they can only employ Jews.”

De Haan quickly reached such prominence that 

Ha’aretz

 labelled him and other Agudah members “traitors” and “scum.” Such words helped fuel the violent attacks of Jewish settler groups against Agudah members to the point where, in 1924, a member of the Haganah, the main Zionist militia, assassinated him. The order was given by Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, later to become the second president of Israel. 

Moser then jumps to Egypt, focusing on Sadiq Saad, an Egyptian, anti-Zionist, Jewish leftist. One of Saad’s most important works was 

Palestine in the Claws of Colonialism, 

published in 1947 and detailing the apartheid-style system then already established. One of the book’s contributions was its coverage of the unique experience of the Palestinian peasantry. Unlike almost all other peasantries, when the Palestinians were expelled from their land, they were denied employment by the new owners of the land or in the cities. This came directly from the policies of the Palestine Foundation Fund, the World Zionist Organisation’s fundraising arm, which specifically stated in its loan contracts that the borrower “pledges to hire Jewish workers only.”

The book covers numerous other examples of prominent anti-Zionist Jewish individuals and groups. The chapters on the immediate post-World War Two period are particularly useful in understanding the rapid transformation of both Zionism and those opposed to it. The French New Left, for example, during the 1950s and 1960s suffered through a period of deep confusion that led many prominent figures to support a form of Zionism. Similarly, the chapter on Reform Judaism in the United States, which had opposed Zionism since the late 19th Century, shows how rapidly the political context changed from the late 1940s, as Moser writes:

“For Americans and other Westerners, the question of Israel’s legitimacy was, for the most part, no longer debated. The feeling that Israel was compensation for the Holocaust became so widespread that the anti-Zionists were mainly forgotten.” 

In barely half a century after Herzl’s 

Der Judenstaat

, support for a Jewish state in Palestine had grown from a fringe movement to a majority view within Western Judaism. And its key practical conclusion of turning Israel into an outpost of Western imperialism in the Middle East had won firm support among the Western ruling classes. 

Moser’s book is one of several in recent years from prominent anti-Zionist and Israel-critical Jewish writers that challenge mainstream narratives on Israel. Avi Shlaim’s 2023 memoir, 

Three Worlds: Memoirs of an Arab-Jew

, tells the story of his family’s expulsion from Iraq in the early 1950s. For generations his family had lived in Baghdad, a city where one-third of the population was Jewish during World War One, and Zionism was almost non-existent.

Shlaim documents how, after 1948, Israeli terrorists bombed several Jewish-owned businesses and a synagogue to foment racial tensions and force the Iraqi Jewish community to emigrate to Israel. At the time, “there had been no other attack on the Jewish community (in Iraq) in recent centuries,” according to Shlaim. From Israel’s founding in 1948 to the first bomb in 1950, only 126 Iraqi Jews had registered to emigrate. But once the attacks began thousands began to register. It took only a few years to put an end to two and a half millennia of Jewish presence in Mesopotamia.

When Shlaim’s family arrived in Israel in 1951, they faced extreme anti-semitism, this time from Israelis who denied them their right to be both Jewish 

and 

Arab. As Israel’s first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion, said “We do not want the Israelis to turn into Arabs.” 

Two other recent examples that focus on Jewish left-wing organisations are Molly Crabapple’s 

Here Where We Live Is Our Country: The Story Of The Jewish Bund

 and Benjamin Balthaser’s 

Citizens of the Whole World: Anti-Zionism and the cultures of the American Jewish left

.

Whilst reading Moser’s book, one cannot help but consider the changes in the Palestine movement over recent years. When Moser arrived at Brown University in the 1990s there was not “any real organized Palestinian presence.” Yet over recent years Ivy League universities have been some of the leading sites of pro-Palestinian resistance. Moser notes that one of the biggest barriers to the Palestine and anti-Zionist movement growing even bigger is the “lack of a tradition to fall back on.” His work, along with the others mentioned above, is an important contribution to re-building such a tradition.

author: Elliot Downes
title: NT government closes Darwin’s largest homelessness shelter
content:
Residents of Darwin’s largest homelessness shelter were evicted by the Northern Territory government on 12 October, and relocated to Batchelor, a town 100 kilometres away.

Yilli Short Stay Accommodation (YiSSA), which is run by Yilli Rreung Housing Aboriginal Corporation, was home to hundreds of people, mostly Aboriginal. Many have experienced domestic violence and are living with serious health conditions, including kidney conditions requiring dialysis. 

Residents from communities across the territory would stay at YiSSA while accessing medical care or other services in Darwin. Nearly 400 people were directly affected by the closure of the facility, including 160 children.

YiSSA’s closure will place more pressure on remaining homelessness services in Darwin. Meanwhile, the minority of residents transferred to the smaller facility in Batchelor will not have the same access to support networks, food, healthcare and education. Batchelor is a town with a population of around 500, a small health clinic and no public transport. 

The closure of a key homelessness service is particularly egregious given the Northern Territory has the highest rate of homelessness in the country. According to data released last year by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 

one in every 25 Territorians requires homelessness assistance

, and Aboriginal people make up 89 percent of those accessing homelessness services in the Northern Territory.

As the biggest landlord in the territory, the Northern Territory government is largely to blame for this situation. Territorians on the emergency public housing waiting list can expect to 

wait up to a decade for a roof over their head

. The government is also responsible for the apartheid-like conditions in Aboriginal town camps on the outskirts of places like Darwin and Alice Springs, as well as the overcrowding in remote communities.

The closure of YiSSA was announced by the ruling Country Liberal Party (CLP) in July. Ostensibly, it was due to a failure to secure a deal with Ausco, the owner of the buildings and other infrastructure on the Crown land site. But in reality, it was a political decision. 

After years of renting the demountable buildings, the government offered to buy them for $3 million—the equivalent of just one year’s rent. When this offer was rejected by Ausco, the federal government proposed to cover the cost of the purchase on the condition that Yilli Rreung continue running the service.

The CLP rejected the offer of federal funding, with Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro calling it a 

“waste of taxpayers’ hard-earned money”

. Yet it has cost 

$16.25 million to establish and fund the Batchelor facility

, run by Mission Australia.

The announcement of YiSSA’s closure sparked a campaign by the activist group, Justice Not Jails (JNJ). It culminated in a 200-strong rally outside of the Australian Homelessness Conference in Darwin just days before residents were to be evicted. 

Anna, an activist with JNJ, told 

Red Flag

 that the decision doesn’t make sense “unless you approach it from an ideological viewpoint. Some of the YiSSA residents have said that [the government] just don’t want Aboriginal people to have a nice, secure place to live.”

The YiSSA closure is symptomatic of a Trumpian government that has targeted Aboriginal people in particular. Since coming to power in 2024, the CLP have lowered the age of criminal responsibility to 10, reintroduced spit hoods in detention, and made it easier for Aboriginal children to be removed from their families and placed into long-term state care.

This has involved a significant expansion in the carceral state, with the prison population 

increasing by 24 percent between 2024 and 2025

, and the Finocchiaro government announcing earlier this year the construction of a new private prison in Darwin. 

The Northern Territory is one of the most incarcerated places in the world, 

second only to El Salvador

, with more than 1 percent of the entire population behind bars. Increasingly, this includes people on remand, who are awaiting trial or sentencing.

According to Anna, the next phase of the campaign will involve putting pressure on the federal Labor government. “There’s been a lot of disagreement between the CLP and Labor about what was actually promised. It’s all really immature and I think disrespectful to the people whose lives are actually being affected,” she told 

Red Flag. 

“The federal government obviously has the money. If they really wanted to do something, they could just purchase [land] and build a facility in Darwin.”

Despite social media posts critical of the YiSSA closure and promises of more consultation with Aboriginal communities, Labor has been in power in the Territory for the majority of the last 25 years and shares responsibility for the housing and incarceration crises. 

What the Northern Territory desperately needs is an organised left-wing force capable of mobilising the opposition to the closure of YiSSA and similar attacks by the Territory government, a force that can draw on the power of organised workers to make it impossible for governments to carry them through. A force willing to stand up to the criminals who run the capitalist system, who see human beings as dispensable if they’re not helping a business or landlord make money. The formation of the NT Socialists is an important step in that direction.

The petition against the YiSSA closure is available 

here

.

author: Danica Rachel
title: Operation Paperclip: The Nazis behind the US space program
content:
The Apollo moon landings are some of the most impressive technical feats ever achieved, and, for capitalism’s boosters, definitive evidence of the superiority of Western capitalism over all other social systems. The United States beating the Soviet Union to the finish line in the space race is held up as the ultimate triumph of capitalism over communism. But the path that took humans to the heavens began in the depths of hell: the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp in Nazi Germany.

Built near the town of Nordhausen in central Germany, Mittelbau-Dora provided its prisoners as slaves to the Mittelwerk. This was a factory built under a mountain for the mass production of the V2 rocket, the world’s first long-range guided ballistic missile. The several thousand civilians killed in London and Antwerp by V2s were not the only victims of these Nazi weapons: at least 20,000 prisoners died as a result of the conditions in Mittelbau-Dora and the Mittelwerk.

Edwin Katzenellenbogen, who was convicted for crimes committed as a doctor at the Buchenwald camp, described Dora as “the Hell of all the concentration camps”. Tens of thousands of prisoners worked in interchanging 12-hour shifts, first to dig the kilometres-long tunnels of the Mittelwerk, then on the dark production lines within.

Sanitation was absent, disease and starvation were rampant, and collective punishment was common. Prisoners were hanged in groups of up to a dozen at a time, and on at least one occasion, bodies were left to dangle over the areas where others were forced to continue working.

Wernher von Braun was an SS officer, scientific director of the V-weapons project, and head of the Mittelbau-Dora planning office. He came from an aristocratic family in the German empire, and was among the first pioneers of advanced rocket science. Through the interwar years, Germany was banned from investing in many kinds of weaponry under the Treaty of Versailles, but rockets were obscure enough to avoid being on the list. During this time, von Braun became a leading designer and inventor of the engines needed to propel explosive missiles over incredible distances.

He joined the Nazi Party in 1937. If you believe his version of events, he joined only to be allowed to continue his scientific work. Regardless of his political loyalty, he was at least comfortable enough with the genocidal policies of the Third Reich to enjoy the slave labour it provided to him from Mittelbau-Dora. He was certainly aware of the reality of the Mittelwerk, having visited the tunnels himself at least ten times.

As the walls closed in on the Third Reich, with US and British forces moving in from the west and Russians from the east, von Braun hid the most important of the design documents for constructing V2s. Alongside Major General Walter Dornberger, head of the German army’s weapons department, von Braun used the hidden documents as leverage to get an amnesty with the Americans, betting that the US wanted the weapons more than they cared about prosecuting war criminals.

He was right. Von Braun, Dornberger and many other German experts in weapons of many terrifying forms—ballistic, chemical, and biological—were brought across the Atlantic under a secret program known as Operation Paperclip. They began work in the US, making weapons for a new, but no less bloodthirsty, empire. Their pasts were whitewashed, with the story being that they were innocent scientists forced by circumstance into working for the Nazi regime.

For his part, Joseph Stalin got the Mittelwerk factory itself, which continued operation for a few years before its machinery was brought back to Russia, along with thousands of German technicians needed to operate it. The USSR also got the equipment and methods to manufacture sarin gas, a chemical weapon so potent that contact with a single droplet causes a painful death.

Sarin was invented by Nazi chemists, among them Otto Ambros, who tested it on Auschwitz prisoners. Ambros was convicted for crimes against humanity in the Nuremberg trials, but that wasn’t a barrier to later working for US chemical companies and the US army. Within a few years of the end of the war, both imperial superpowers were producing large quantities of sarin and other chemical weapons.

The Cold War and the arms race 

The new phase of world imperialism had the globe divided into the West, with the US on top, against the East orbiting the USSR. The prospect of direct hot war between the empires gave way to the Cold War, and the arms race continued. Both sides had nuclear and thermonuclear bombs, the most destructive weapons ever created. The next step was to be able to use them to precisely target any location on Earth.

The idea of an intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) being fired between continents, from Europe to America or vice versa, drove weapons development in the immediate postwar years. Rocket science was central to this, and the Nazi V2 was to become the ancestor of modern rocketry.

Space exploration was tied up with the race to ICBMs from the beginning. Von Braun himself was obsessed with concepts of lunar bases and hypothetical expeditions to Mars. The launch of the Russian satellite Sputnik in October 1957, the first artificial object put into orbit, was the starter’s gun for the space race.

Sputnik really showed up the US, which had been coasting on the assumption that it was ahead. Sputnik proved that in fact the USSR was winning the race in space technology and also in ICBMs—they had used one to launch Sputnik. NASA, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, was established the next year. The US launched its own satellite in February 1958, only four months after Sputnik.

In September 1962, US President John F. Kennedy announced his government’s intention to send men to the moon in a speech at Rice University. The famous words, “we choose to go to the moon … not because [it is] easy, but because [it is] hard”, were preceded by Orwellian double-speak about how the US must “occupy a position of pre-eminence” in space to preserve “peace”. That is, the US must win this arms race so that no other empire would be able to dominate the planet. As JFK spoke, the US military was escalating its war in Vietnam.

The US would proceed to be beaten to every major milestone in the space race except for boots on the moon itself: the first artificial satellite, the first animal in space, the first human in space, and the first spacewalk were all accomplished by the USSR.

The advantage that NASA had over Moscow was von Braun and the other Nazi rocket scientists, who were the world’s leading experts. Former high-ranking Nazis were involved in every significant US development in space and rocket technology in the course of the space race.

In 1954, Bell Labs created the first guided surface-to-air missile. This was developed by Dornberger, who would go on to be vice-president of the Bell Aircraft corporation and a consultant for Boeing.

In 1958, America’s first satellite was launched on a rocket designed by von Braun. He would be the first director of the Marshall Space Flight Center, NASA’s main base of operations for rocket research.

Kurt Debus was the first director of NASA’s Launch Center. He oversaw the launches of the first US satellite, the first American in space, and all of the Apollo mission launches. He was well qualified, because overseeing launches of rockets was the job Hitler gave him as an SS officer.

And the famous Saturn V rockets that propelled the Apollo missions were developed under the management of Arthur Rudolph, former deputy head of V2 production at the Mittelwerk. Von Braun, of course, was also centrally involved.

The developments made in rocketry that were needed for the space program were the same developments needed for the US to be able to build ICBMs. The goal of landing a rocket on the moon instead of on Moscow, and delivering explorers instead of nuclear warheads, was ultimately just a gloss over what was really weapons research for the Cold War.

The Paperclip scientists did not fall into obscurity as nameless technicians. Many of them became very public leaders of the US space program, and hardcore advocates for the militarisation of space.

Von Braun in particular was a prolific writer for science magazines. A 1952 issue of the magazine 

Collier’s

, featuring articles under the heading “Man Will Conquer Space Soon”, inspired Walt Disney to get in touch with him. The Nazi rocket expert helped to design parts of Disneyland and consulted for TV specials produced by Disney. After the space race, von Braun was a consulting editor for 

Popular Science

, one of the US’s most widely-read science magazines, until his death in 1977.

The truth about von Braun and his colleagues is today widely acknowledged. But that doesn’t stop many from continuing to venerate him, with his leadership role in NASA being his main legacy. The National Space Society, a US space science non-profit, has awarded the “Wernher von Braun Memorial Award” every second year since 1993 to recognise “excellence in management of and leadership for a space-related project”. Past recipients include Elon Musk and current NASA administrator Jared Isaacman.

What is less remembered is Mittelbau-Dora and the tens of thousands of innocent lives lost there. It is a tragedy of history that the name Wernher von Braun is known more than the names of those like Jean Michel.

Resistance

Michel was an organiser in the French Resistance against Nazi occupation. He was arrested by the Gestapo in 1943 and ended up in Mittelbau-Dora, where he spent close to two years. His memoir, 

Dora

, is both horrifying in its stories of the cruelty of the Nazi regime, and one of the most inspiring tales of resistance available.

Even in the deepest darkness the spirits of Michel and other prisoners were never broken. Secret networks organised sabotage on the V2 production lines, snuck in to SS quarters to listen to British broadcasts on the radio, and spread news about the advance of the Allied armies towards Germany. They even constructed a radio transmitter they planned to use to call for help when those armies got close enough.

No telling of the story of space exploration should be considered complete without beginning with Mittelbau-Dora. Not only is it the starting point, it is also emblematic of what is at the heart of competition over space. The driving force behind Nazi rocket science was the same force behind the space races of the Cold War and today: imperial domination and all the violence that comes with it.

This September, the US confirmed publicly for the first time that it has deployed weapons into orbit around Earth. More missions to the moon are planned by today’s biggest powers, the US and China. Capitalism continues to walk down the pathway to the final frontier that began at Mittelbau-Dora, and each step brings the threat of all-out war closer.

title: Palestine supporters guilty once again, declares Murdoch press

author: Luca Tavan
title: Europe’s youth and workers in revolt
content:
The metaphor of a tinderbox is one of the most overused in politics. But how else could you describe the situation in Europe today, where every small spark of resistance seems to be catching and turning into a powerful blaze? 

Things kicked off in France in late September, when students in the working-class suburb of Créteil in the South-east of Paris blockaded their school in protest against poor conditions. This has since grown into the deepest challenge French President Emmanuel Macron has faced in his ten years in power. On October 17, students were joined by workers in a national mobilisation of 800,000. Strikes, demonstrations, blockades and riots have all played a role in this movement. It’s not just the radical left comparing this situation to the legendary student and worker uprising of May 1968.

In Spain, anger at the eviction of María del Carmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman whose rent was raised 230 percent when her apartment was acquired by an investment firm, has generated a massive movement for housing justice. The streets have forced the centre-left Sanchez government to call early elections, and typically hesitant union leaders to schedule a general strike for November 11. 

Protests have rocked Albania since May, in response to an environmentally catastrophic luxury resort development tied to the Trump family. On October 13, youth inspired by the French protests brought their own demands over education and wages into the mix, turning the movement into a national uprising. Government buildings have been invaded and burnt, and the call for the downfall of Edi Rama’s government is widespread. It is the country’s largest revolt since the fall of Stalinist regime in the early 1990s.  

In Italy, mass protests pledging to “fare come in Francia” (to do as in France) last weekend turned into standoffs against the police. In Milan, 250 people were detained, more than 80 percent of whom were minors. Belgium, Portugal, and Ireland have seen mass protests and strikes taking aim at austerity and intolerable working conditions. 

This marks the biggest wave of protests on the continent in at least a generation. Anyone who wants to see capitalism one day toppled and replaced with a system really fit for human beings should take great hope from these events. 

There’s no telling how long these struggles will continue, whether they will lose momentum, or if massive state repression will succeed in intimidating many off the streets. But this convergence of different struggles provides a glimpse of the possibility of rebuilding class-based politics after a decade characterised by despair and far right ascendancy. 

The roots of the revolt 

While these different movements are profoundly shaped by their specific national contexts, they have common roots in decades of battered living standards and attacks on workers. An entire generation suffered the consequences of the 2008 economic crisis - wages were slashed, young people were left without the prospect of ever finding a job, and social services were gutted to bail out the banks. 

Italy provides perhaps the sharpest example of the consequences of this class war waged by the rich: according to data from Italy's Parliamentary Budget Office, private sector workers have seen their real wages fall by 6.6 percent between 1990 and 2026. 

In countries experiencing economic recovery, young people are learning that they bear the costs of boom as well as bust. New jobs created are insecure, and wage increases are offset by soaring housing costs. 

This long, bitter experience has brought questions of social class back to the fore and changed the character of struggle. A comparison of the current occupation of Madrid’s Puerta del Sol with the last one is instructive. 2011’s 

Indignados

movement shared many characteristics with the protests of today, fuelled by anger at low wages, evictions and the callousness of the political class. It was an inspiring and important moment for the left. But the politics of the movement were organically populist, seeking to build a cross-class alliance of Spanish ‘citizens’ against the political caste they blamed for the country’s ruin. The most popular slogans reflected this - like “real democracy now!” and “they don’t represent us”. 

This sentiment was also expressed in a hostility to the organised left and workers’ movement within the occupation - seen by many participants as just another facet of the “politics” they felt alienated from. Unions and left parties were even banned by the movement from participating in its marches. This tragically misguided decision put real limits on the extent to which the struggle could deepen and spread from the square to the workplaces. 

Today, the movement is consciously associated with the traditions of the left and working-class struggle. One of the most popular slogans is “Long live the struggle of the working class,”, and visitors to the occupation in Puerta del Sol are greeted with the banners of the radical left, from the anarchist CNT to the Coordinadora Juvenil Socialista (Socialist Youth). They can even take a walk down a thoroughfare protesters have named the “Paseo de Rosa Luxemburg.” 

It’s also not surprising that youth in general, and students in particular, have been the leavening agent and the detonator of so many of these struggles. Young people have been the motor behind every great movement of historical change over the history of capitalism.

Today, the lives of a new generation are being shaped by an alarming new political context - characterised not just by class attacks, but also by the reorganisation of world capitalism around rising war and authoritarianism. 

That militarism and austerity are just two sides of the same coin is clear to student protesters in France: the government is attempting to pass €54 billion in social spending cuts, while boasting that they are ahead of schedule with plans to double military spending. German students resisting the potential reintroduction of conscription have made the same connection, with chants like “The rich want war, the youth want a future” and “Our only war is the class war”. 

Ruling-class hypocrites sermonise about violence 

Much of the domestic response to these movements and international commentary has focused on rioting and alleged “violence” of some demonstrators. In a televised address over the weekend, Emmanuel Macron criticised what he called ‘unbridled violence’, asking “how could French people do this to France?”

But much of this ‘violence’ is a response to brutal state repression, a fact which warrants little attention in mainstream media coverage. In France, riots were provoked by outrageous police tactics. One 

eyewitness

 account describes: “officers patrolled in groups of four or five mopeds, each carrying a pair of armed officers. One officer stands ready to jump off, beat protesters indiscriminately and speed away before anyone can retaliate.”

The denunciation of violence is particularly ironic from the French president. Macron currently enjoys a narrower social base than many dictatorships (a recent Ipsos BVA-Cesi survey found that 82 percent disapproved of his performance) and has only been able to hold on to power through the routine and systematic use of violence. In the current wave of protests, one student has lost a hand, one an arm, another an eye. 

There has also been much establishment consternation about property damage, particularly after the burning of the historic town hall in the French town of Limonge. Karl

 

Marx wrote on this theme 150 years ago, as troops moved in to crush the Paris Commune, murdering thousands of workers: “The bourgeoisie of the whole world, which looks complacently upon the wholesale massacre after the battle, is convulsed by horror at the desecration of brick and mortar!” 

Those who rule over a system based on such brutal violence are in no position to remonstrate about the rights of buildings. 

If many of the participants in these movements are willing to defend a variety of forms of resistance, from the strike to the blockade to the riot, it’s because of an inevitable impatience that comes from learning how far you get when you go through the “proper channels.”  Anjeza Marku, an Albanian student, told the Austrian newspaper 

Der Standard

: L

“We protested peacefully for 135 days, but those in power merely insulted the participants. The public sees the youth as Albania’s last hope—we have often even been compared to the youth in France. But the government couldn’t care less whether we protest peacefully. It won’t listen to our voices anyway”.

Repression and racism 

The establishment's focus on the supposed violence of these movements has two aims. First, to criminalise resistance, and second, for a wing of the ruling class, to racialise it in public consciousness. 

The response of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government is typical. It has sent 500 additional troops to Milan and rushed through a new “security decree” further penalising protests and allowing for 

preventive detention of minors

. 

At the same time, the government and their right-wing backers in the media have made a concerted attempt to blame the unrest on “maranza, a racist slur for groups of North African youth in working class suburbs. Deputy Premier Matteo Salvini complained the squares were filled with “maranza and rotten left-wing riff-raff.” and has threatened to strip Italian-born migrants who riot of their citizenship rights. Businessman and current Defence Minister Guido Crosetto has accused youth of waging a ‘hybrid war’ against Italian society. 

The reason migrant youth have had a prominent place in the demonstrations is obvious. Working-class migrants have to suffer the double blow of economic exploitation and racist humiliation. Moroccan youth who faced down heavily armed police in Bologna last weekend weren’t doing so for the first time. In July, the city saw its own “George Floyd'” moment, when protests erupted after police killed Abderrahim Fakir, a Moroccan migrant suffering a psychiatric episode. Migrants living in Fakir’s neighbourhood of Pilastro are used to being targeted. During 2020 regional elections, Matteo Salvini performed a stunt in the area where he rang the bell of a Tunisian family’s home to ask them over the intercom if they were drug dealers. No wonder that when resistance breaks out, people who are so beaten and repressed rush to the front lines. 

This racialised authoritarian response is being carried by the far right from Europe across the world. Trump addressed a Kansas rally on Tuesday to denounce the movement and describe France as a country “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists.” Here in Australia, Pauline Hanson has warned: “Unless Australia stops importing people who reject our democracy, our way of life … these riots will eventually be coming to Australian cities”. Sky News has attempted to draw the link between the European revolt and sinister forces at home, with segments like: “Pro-Palestine rioters ‘energised’ by anti-West sentiments.” The right-wing press has hysterically denounced an upcoming student strike against Hanson on November 11, accusing the high-schoolers of planning a “France-style riot.” 

The sharp divergence of responses to this wave of revolt, described either as the great hope for a more just world or a terrifying plot to Islamicise the west, reflects the depth of the political polarisation that has been produced. But it also reflects the asymmetry of that polarisation, one in which the far right is several orders of magnitude stronger than the left and has had its conspiratorial and fascistic worldview embraced as a permanent and legitimate wing of capitalist politics. The radicalisation on the right continues to build. In Italy where Meloni’s far-right coalition is losing its lustre, it now faces a challenge in the form of the hardline fascist Futuro Nazionale, led by retired army general Roberto Vanacci.

Challenges for the left 

These hopeful struggles in Europe have emerged in a pretty bleak period. The ascendancy of the far right and multiplying horrors of capitalism are felt especially by people on the left who are aware of the long-term challenges for our side. Decades of defeat, demoralisation and working-class disorganisation have had a profound impact on the politics of the left. One reflection of this has been the tendency for socialists to lower their horizons and adapt to the politics of the centre-left, accepting Spain’s Pedro Sanchez or Brazil’s Lula da Silva as the height of their ambition. 

Another expression of this demoralisation is the retreat in some left-wing circles into doomerism and crisis-mongering, emphasising the potentially apocalyptic direction of world capitalism without an argument about how the forces to resist it could be built.

These struggles show another possibility. They are a vindication of Marxism’s central claim: that the functioning of capitalism contains within it potentially explosive contradictions, which can rapidly burst onto the scene. The capitalist system can never come good on its promises of a good life for the majority. And the potential power of the masses of people that have no real stake in this rotten order can be obscured and repressed, but it can never be eradicated. 

People are driven to act again and again. This is the only thing that can open up the possibility not just winning immediate gains but also creating ideological fissures which can lead to a break with the dominant order. Lenin reflected on this basic point after the failed revolution of 1905:

“Only struggle educates the exploited class. Only struggle discloses to it the magnitude of its own power, widens its horizon, enhances its abilities, clarifies its mind, forges its will.”

But it’s not enough to champion resistance. The challenge for socialists is not only to act as participants, but to try to give shape and direction to it and argue for a way forward. There will be many obstacles on the road to deepening these struggles, including opportunistic capitalist politicians who want to ride these movements into power, as in Albania, and conservative union leaders who only want strikes according to a neatly planned timetable, as in Spain and France.  

The last great wave of European revolt in 2011 generated exciting new possibilities. But ultimately the political forces it generated led things to disaster. In Spain, the populist party Podemos channelled resistance in a parliamentary direction and ultimately ended up in coalition with the centre-left they pledged to replace. In Greece, a party that emerged as a coalition of the radical left ended up forming a government, only to rapidly capitulate to the financial pressure of the ruling class and become as bad as the centre parties they had denounced.  

But despite the weight of so many crushing defeats, a new generation is standing up and grasping toward radical solutions to the radical problems posed by capitalism. The challenge for socialists is to grab hold of this opportunity and begin building the forces for revolution in the 21st century.

title: Striking for Palestine in Aotearoa
content:
Thousands of workers at universities and polytechnics (TAFEs) across Aotearoa (New Zealand) went on strike Wednesday 21 October, rallying against poor pay offers and the increasing precarity of employment in tertiary education. Now tertiary workers join teachers, public servants, health workers and others who have taken action over the last two years.

author: Robert Narai
title: Hungary 1956: a workers’ revolution against Stalinism
content:
Seventy years ago, Hungarian workers and students rose up against a brutal dictatorship that justified itself in the language of Marxism. In its place, they built workers’ councils: organs of working-class democracy, giving future generations a chance to discover the essence of revolutionary Marxism.

My grandfather, Vendel Koroknai, often played Beethoven’s Egmont Overture on his record player and spoke fondly of its role in the 1956 revolution. The overture tells the story of Lamoral, count of Egmont, who defied Spanish tyranny under the duke of Alba. His execution sparked a broader rebellion that led to Dutch independence. For the Hungarians who heard it, the parallels were striking: the Russians as the oppressive occupiers, themselves as the Dutch seeking self-determination.

They heard it because on the evening of 23 October 1956, workers and students defeated the hated AVH, the secret police of the dictatorship that had ruled Hungary for the previous eight years, in fierce street fighting and gun battles, and took control of Magyar Radio in central Budapest.
